newsitem.title: JAPAN: TOKYO STOCKS SEEN DRIFTING, EYES ON FUJI TV LISTING.
newsitem.headline: TOKYO STOCKS SEEN DRIFTING, EYES ON FUJI TV LISTING.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are seen drifting on Friday, with market interest focused on the scheduled listing of Fuji Television Network Inc, brokers said.

They added although most of the market was likely to be preoccupied with Fuji's debut, worries about the health of some firms in the battered construction sector would persist. Items such as Japan's cur surplus data for the first half of 1997, forecasts for machinery orders and the options settlement could also affect the market, they said.
On Thursday, the Nikkei average finished below the 19,500 level for the first time since May 1.
It closed 226.22 points or 1.15 percent lower at 19,475.85. September Nikkei futures fell 380 points to end at 19,370.
"Fuji TV is the biggest thing on the agenda today," Sanyo Securities' general manager, Mitsuru Hayashino, said. "How the shares do today could influence the entire stock market."
The initial offer price of Fuji TV shares is 550,000 yen. Brokers expect the share price to rise above the weighted average price of 615,735 yen.
But they said that there were many uncertainties concerning the supply/demand situation of the shares as Nomura Securities Co Ltd was out of the market.
Japan's largest broker is being penalised for its illegal dealings with a corporate racketeer.
Fuji TV's lead manager is Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd which is also suspected of having links with the same racketeer at the heart of the Nomura scandal.

"Yamaichi was under suspicion and was even raided, which means that they may not have been able to advertise the shares aggressively enough," one broker said. Market sources envision a range of 19,200 to 19,700 for the Nikkei average in the Friday session.

Brokers said although the market was relieved about Fuji TV, other niggling worries, especially about the health of the construction sector and the future of the economy, were dragging down the indices.
"Builders are dominating the percentage loser list and shares which are at levels usually occupied by those going bust are not showing signs of reviving," Shimizu said.
Constructor Aoki Corp stood at 61 yen, up one.
Brokers said the elimination of cross shareholdings and a gloomy outlook on the economy were hanging over large capital issues and those of firms dependent on domestic demand.
"The economy seems to be worsening and the need to sell shares of raw materials firms such as Nippon Steel Corp is strengthening," a "Big Four" broker said.
Nippon Steel shares fell 13 yen to 298 and was the second most heavily traded issue with volume of 6.91 million shares.
Data showing Japan's current account surplus up 55.8 percent in June from a year earlier was within expectations and did not provide much direction for the market.
"There are numerous things on the agenda such as machinery order forecasts in addition to the Fuji TV listing," a trader said. "Investors may be too preoccupied to trade actively."
By sector, precision instruments and real estate were the only sectors posting major gains. Communications, fisheries, iron/steel, rubber and mining were at the top of the list of decliners.
TOPIX fell 13.93 points or 0.93 percent to 1,483.17. The Nikkei 300 shed 2.63 points or 0.90 percent to reach 290.40.
--Masako Iijima, Tokyo Equities Desk (+81-3-3432-9052
